analysis.one_liner: Commercial website operator is unlawful to collect personal information without notice and opt-out.
analysis.headline: Online privacy bill requiring websites to notify users and let them limit use of their personal data was referred to committee, held one hearing, and died without a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Would have required commercial websites to tell users what personal info they collect, how it's used, who it's sold to, and let users opt out of marketing uses and third-party disclosure. FTC enforcement, $22,000 civil penalties per violation, capped at $500,000 per related series; state AGs could sue; safe harbor for FTC-approved self-regulatory seal programs; preempts stronger state laws. Also directs a $1M NRC study of online privacy.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users — notice and opt-out for marketing/third-party disclosure of their personal data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users whose data is collected

how_it_helps.text: Websites must give clear, conspicuous notice of what data is collected, whether it's sold to third parties, and how to opt out.
Users get an online opportunity to limit marketing use and third-party disclosure of information not needed for the product or service.
Violations carry civil penalties up to $22,000 each (capped at $500,000 per related series) and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of residents.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial website operators and online advertisers/marketers, who would face compliance costs and lose unrestricted resale of user data; FTC and partner agencies bear enforcement costs.

drawbacks.text: Preempts stronger state privacy laws, capping protections at the federal floor.
Safe harbor lets FTC-approved industry self-regulatory seal programs substitute for legal compliance, softening enforcement.
Notice-and-opt-out model leaves default data collection in place; users must act to protect themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Meaningful privacy gains for consumers, though notice-and-opt-out plus industry safe harbors blunt the impact.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Commerce Committee on introduction; one hearing in October 2000; no markup, no floor vote, died when the 106th Congress ended January 2001.

narrative.text: Introduced July 26, 2000 by McCain with Kerry, Abraham, and Boxer; read twice and referred to Commerce Committee.
Committee held hearings October 3, 2000 (S.Hrg. 106-1147); no further action before Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online advertisers and data brokers kept collecting and selling personal data without notice-and-opt-out requirements; no floor vote was ever taken despite bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired the committee that held its only hearing.

for.name: Sens. John Kerry, Spencer Abraham, and Barbara Boxer

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Held a hearing but never brought the bill to a markup or floor vote
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee, held one hearing in October 2000, then took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Bipartisan sponsorship (Republican sponsor, Democratic and Republican cosponsors) with no recorded floor opposition — the bill simply never advanced.

industries.industry: Online advertisers, data brokers, and commercial websites
industries.note: Would face compliance costs and lose unrestricted resale of user data for marketing. Its interest in killing the bill ran against consumers' interest in data protection.
